c.tagline: Pearl of the Pacific: Mexico's longest malecón, a colorful Old Town, and Carnival by the sea.

taxi.fareNote: Fares are not metered — agree the price before getting in. Mazatlán's signature 'pulmonías' (open-air VW-based carts) and larger 'aurigas' pickups run alongside regular taxis; Uber and DiDi also operate and are often cheaper.

emergency.note: 911 is Mexico's unified emergency number for police, fire, and ambulance; 078 is the national tourist assistance line.

avoid.reason: Tourist "Golden Zone" safe; caution in the centre at night; Sinaloa cartel presence — avoid drugs

hood_desc: Mazatlán's restored 19th-century heart around Plazuela Machado and the Angela Peralta Theatre, full of colorful merchant mansions, galleries, cafes and the city's best restaurants; the top pick for culture and walkability.

The Golden Zone is the main resort strip — a few miles of high-rise beach hotels, souvenir shops, bars and nightclubs fronting popular swimming beaches; suits first-timers who want everything sun-and-fun in one place.
A modern, upscale district of canals, a yacht marina, golf and newer condo resorts north of the Golden Zone; calm and polished, better for drivers than for those wanting to walk everywhere.
A quieter, more residential beach area at the northern end of the bay with wide sands and surf; good for families and longer stays wanting space away from the resort crowds.
lodging: Pueblo Bonito Vantage Centro Histórico Mazatlán

water.note: Stick to bottled or purified water despite local claims the supply is potable.

transit.hours: City buses run roughly 5:00am to 10:30pm; pulmonías and taxis fill the late-night gaps.
transit.note: There is no metro or rail; getting around means cheap city buses, Mazatlán's open-air 'pulmonía' carts, regular taxis and ride apps, plus a long seafront Malecón that's easy to walk or cycle.
transit.pay: City buses are paid in cash to the driver (about MXN 10-13, ~US$0.70); there is no rechargeable transit card. Pulmonías and taxis are paid in cash at a negotiated flat fare.

bus: Central de Autobuses de Mazatlán (main intercity bus terminal)
ferry: Baja Ferries (Mazatlán–La Paz, Baja California Sur)

tip.r: Around 10-15% at restaurants is customary; tip pulmonía drivers, bartenders and tour guides in cash.

places.name: Costa Marinera
places.note: Beachfront kitchen keeping Sinaloan recipes straight, with sunset seating.

places.name: Puerto Azul
places.note: Locals name it first for seafood; the black aguachile is worth the heat.

food.name: Pescado zarandeado
food.desc: A whole butterflied snapper rubbed with chilli and mayonnaise-mustard marinade, clamped in a grate and grilled slowly over mangrove coals.

places.name: Puerto Azul
places.note: Widely considered the city's benchmark zarandeado; order for two or more.

places.name: Mariscos El Cuchupetas
places.note: Charcoal-grilled whole fish served family-style with tortillas and salsas.

places.name: Costa Marinera
places.note: Does the classic Sinaloan marinade and serves it with the shell-on shrimp sides.

food.name: Tacos de camaron and tacos gobernador
food.desc: Griddled shrimp tacos, and the Mazatlan-invented gobernador - shrimp, melted cheese and poblano folded into a crisped tortilla.

places.name: Costa Marinera
places.note: Tacos gobernador are a house specialty and made to the original formula.

places.name: El Muchacho Alegre
places.note: Lively seafood house with music and Pacific views; good for a taco-and-beer night.

places.name: Mercado Jose Maria Pino Suarez
places.note: Century-old market with taco and tostada counters aimed at locals, not tourists.

food.name: Ceviche mazatleco
food.desc: Finely chopped fish or shrimp cured in lime with tomato, onion and coriander, piled on tostadas with hot sauce and avocado.

places.name: La Puntilla
places.note: Harbour-side spot by the ferry terminal, watching the shrimp boats unload.

places.name: Mariscos El Cuchupetas
places.note: Enormous ceviche and callo de hacha platters at local prices.

places.name: Costa Marinera
places.note: Mazatlan-style ceviche kept simple and citrus-forward.

food.name: Marlin ahumado
food.desc: Smoked marlin shredded with tomato and chilli, served as tacos, tostadas or empanadas - a Mazatlan bar snack and market staple.

places.name: Mercado Jose Maria Pino Suarez
places.note: Stalls sell smoked marlin by weight plus ready-made tacos and empanadas.

places.name: La Puntilla
places.note: Smoked marlin tacos alongside the day's catch, near the port.

places.name: Mariscos El Cuchupetas
places.note: Smoked marlin empanadas make a good starter before the grilled fish.

food.name: Chilorio and Sinaloan home cooking
food.desc: Slow-cooked pork shredded and fried in chilli paste, eaten in tacos or with beans - the inland Sinaloan counterweight to all the seafood.

places.name: El Tunel
places.note: Open since 1945 opposite the Angela Peralta theatre; old-school Sinaloan plates.

places.name: Panama Centro
places.note: Sinaloan bakery-restaurant chain locals use for breakfast, chilorio and pan dulce.

places.name: Mercado Jose Maria Pino Suarez
places.note: Fondas upstairs and around the edges serve daily home-style comidas.

food.name: Cerveza Pacifico
food.desc: The pale lager brewed in Mazatlan since 1900, drunk ice cold from the bottle or as a michelada with lime, chilli and clam juice.

places.name: Pedro y Lola
places.note: Terrace on the old town's prettiest square, with live music most nights.

places.name: La Copa de Leche
places.note: Historic seafront cafe-bar on the malecon, good for a sunset beer.

places.name: Casa Etnika
places.note: Courtyard bar-restaurant in a restored house, mixing beers with local music.

food.name: Tejuino and aguas frescas
food.desc: Fermented corn tejuino served with lime, salt and lime sorbet, plus jamaica, horchata and cebada from carts along the seafront.

places.note: Vendors work the seafront promenade all afternoon; ask for it with nieve de limon.

places.name: Mercado Jose Maria Pino Suarez

places.name: Plazuela Machado stands

landmarks: The Malecón
One of the world's longest seafront promenades curves 21 kilometers past monuments, cliff divers and Pacific sunsets that set the sky ablaze.
El Faro (Faro Mazatlán)
Perched on Cerro del Crestón, one of the world's highest natural lighthouses rewards climbers with a vertiginous glass-floored lookout over the harbor.
Plazuela Machado
The romantic heart of Old Mazatlán, a 19th-century square where sidewalk cafés and pastel colonial facades glow beneath strings of lights.
Teatro Ángela Peralta
A lovingly restored 1874 opera house named for Mexico's 'Nightingale', its neoclassical tiers hosting everything from ballet to Carnaval galas.
Catedral Basílica de la Inmaculada Concepción
Mazatlán's twin-spired 19th-century cathedral dazzles with a gilded baroque interior and unusual Star of David stained-glass windows.
El Clavadista (Cliff Divers at Glorieta Sánchez Taboada)
Local daredevils plunge from a rocky malecón platform into shallow surging waves, a heart-stopping Mazatlán tradition since the 1920s.
Mercado Pino Suárez
An 1899 iron-framed market hall stacked with mangoes, shrimp and leatherwork, the aromatic engine room of downtown Mazatlán life.
Isla de la Piedra (Stone Island)
A short panga ride delivers coconut groves, horseback rides and grilled-fish palapas along one of the region's longest uncrowded beaches.
Zona Dorada
The Golden Zone's resort-lined beaches, from Playa Gaviotas onward, deliver classic parasailing, banda music and margarita-fueled Pacific afternoons.
Olas Altas
The crescent bay where Mazatlán tourism began, its retro hotels, Carnaval monuments and surfable waves steeped in old-school seaside nostalgia.

train.note: Mazatlán has no passenger rail service.

bus.note: Frequent long-distance coaches (TAP, Elite, TUFESA) run from the Central de Autobuses to Guadalajara (~7 hrs), Durango (~3 hrs via the 'Espinazo del Diablo' highway), Culiacán, Tepic and Tijuana; there are no scheduled international coach services.

intl.to: La Paz, Baja California Sur (Mexico) - overnight across the Sea of Cortez, 12-15 hr

ferry.note: Baja Ferries sails overnight across the Sea of Cortez from Mazatlán to La Paz in Baja California Sur (~12-15 hrs), carrying passengers and vehicles.

half.name: El Quelite
half.blurb: A tidy traditional Sinaloan village of cobbled lanes, a famous country restaurant and the ancient ballgame of ulama.

full.name: Copala
full.blurb: A 16th-century colonial silver-mining town in the Sierra Madre foothills, with a cobbled plaza and a hilltop church.

full.name: Concordia
full.blurb: A colonial town known for its baroque San Sebastián church, hand-thrown pottery and carved furniture.
